lessons.title: Climate-Smart Cassava Farming Practices
lessons.body: Climate-smart cassava farming means growing more cassava while adapting to changing weather and reducing greenhouse gases. In Africa, rainfall is becoming unpredictable, and droughts are more common. To be climate-smart, start with the right variety. Improved varieties like TME 419, TMS 30572, and TMS 98/0581 are drought-tolerant and give 20-30 tonnes per hectare with good management. Plant at the onset of rains, using healthy stem cuttings of 20-30 cm with at least 5 nodes. Space 1m by 1m for sole cassava, or 1m by 0.5m if you want to intercrop with legumes like cowpea or groundnut. Intercropping covers the soil, reduces evaporation, and fixes nitrogen. Use minimum tillage to keep soil carbon. Instead of burning, mulch with cassava leaves and crop residues. If you have irrigation, use drip lines to apply water directly to roots. On flat land, build contour ridges to harvest rainwater. In dry areas, plant early maturing varieties like TMS 91/02324 that mature in 9-12 months. Climate-smart also means reducing methane from livestock and using organic fertiliser. Apply 5-10 tonnes of compost or poultry manure per hectare. This improves soil water holding capacity. Rotate cassava with maize or legumes to break pest cycles. After harvest, leave some residues and plant cover crops like mucuna. These practices increase yields, reduce risk, and help fight climate change. Start small: test on one plot, then expand.

lessons.title: Soil Health and Environmental Sustainability
lessons.body: Cassava is tough, but it still needs healthy soil. Continuous cassava farming without adding nutrients depletes the soil. In Africa, many farmers get only 8-10 tonnes per hectare because soils are poor. To sustain production, you must feed the soil. First, test your soil. Contact your local agricultural extension officer or use a simple soil test kit (available from agro-dealers for about $20). Test for pH, nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. Cassava grows best at pH 5.5-6.5. If pH is below 5.0, apply agricultural lime at 1-2 tonnes per hectare. Add organic matter: compost, farmyard manure, or green manure. A good practice is to apply 5 tonnes of manure per hectare before planting. After planting, apply 300 kg per hectare of NPK 15-15-15 at 8 weeks. But don't rely only on chemical fertiliser. Use crop rotation: plant cassava after a legume like soybean or groundnut. Legumes fix nitrogen, reducing the need for fertiliser. Also, avoid burning. Burning destroys organic matter and kills beneficial microbes. Instead, incorporate residues into the soil. Control erosion by planting on contours or using vetiver grass barriers. Keep a cover crop like mucuna between rows. For sustainable harvesting, don't uproot all plants at once; harvest selectively. After 3-4 years, rotate to another crop. These practices maintain soil fertility, reduce costs, and protect the environment. Healthy soil means higher yields and better income.

lessons.title: Mechanization and Digital Tools in Cassava
lessons.body: Mechanization saves labour and increases efficiency. In Africa, most cassava is planted and harvested by hand, which is slow and expensive. A simple tool like a cassava planter (e.g., the IITA motorised planter) can plant 1 hectare in 4 hours instead of 4 days. For harvesting, a tractor-mounted cassava harvester (like the one from AMTEC in Nigeria) can lift 1 hectare per day, reducing labour by 80%. But you don't need a tractor to start. Use a hand-pushed cassava grater or a motorised grater for processing. For weeding, a simple wheel hoe or a knapsack sprayer with herbicide (like glyphosate) can help. Digital tools are also changing cassava farming. Use a mobile phone to access weather forecasts from services like Ignitia or the Kenya Meteorological Department. Apps like FarmDrive or Esoko send market prices and agronomic tips via SMS. You can use a smartphone with GPS to map your farm and track planting dates. For pest and disease identification, use the PlantVillage app or the Cassava Diagnostic app from IITA. These tools are often free. If you have internet, join WhatsApp groups of cassava farmers to share knowledge. For record keeping, use a simple notebook or an app like FarmBook. Start with one tool, like a soil moisture meter ($15) to decide when to irrigate. Mechanisation and digital tools reduce drudgery, increase yields, and help you make better decisions. Invest in what you can afford, and upgrade over time.

lessons.title: Waste Utilization and Circular Economy
lessons.body: Cassava processing generates a lot of waste: peels, wastewater, and bagasse (fibrous residue). Instead of throwing it away, turn it into value. Cassava peels can be dried and milled into animal feed. A simple solar dryer or sun-drying on a raised platform takes 2-3 days. The dried peels contain 10-12% protein and can replace up to 30% of maize in poultry or pig feed. You can sell a 50 kg bag for $5-10. Wastewater from garri processing is rich in starch. Let it settle in a pond, then collect the starch sediment. Dry it and sell as cassava starch for making glue, biscuits, or ethanol. The remaining water can be used to irrigate vegetables after treatment. Bagasse can be used as fuel for cooking or as substrate for mushroom farming. In a circular economy, nothing is wasted. For example, a medium-scale garri processor producing 1 tonne per day generates about 200 kg of peels and 500 litres of wastewater. By converting peels to feed and starch, you can earn an extra $20-30 per day. Also, use cassava leaves as a protein-rich vegetable for human consumption (after proper cooking to remove cyanide). Or make silage for cattle. Start small: build a simple drying rack and a settling pond. Train your workers to separate waste. This reduces environmental pollution and creates new income streams. Circular economy is good for your pocket and the planet.

lessons.title: Research and Development Trends
lessons.body: Research is constantly improving cassava. In Africa, IITA, CIAT, and national programs like NRCRI (Nigeria) and NARO (Uganda) are developing new varieties. Recent trends include biofortified cassava with higher vitamin A (e.g., TMS 07/0593, yellow-fleshed) to fight malnutrition. There are also varieties resistant to cassava mosaic disease (CMD) and cassava brown streak disease (CBSD), like TME 14. Another trend is gene editing to reduce cyanide content, making cassava safer. For farmers, these mean higher yields and better health. Research also focuses on mechanisation: low-cost harvesters and planters are being tested. Digital tools like remote sensing and drones are used to monitor crop health. For example, drones can detect drought stress early. On the processing side, researchers are developing efficient garri fryers and starch extractors. You can access these innovations through extension services, farmer field schools, and agricultural shows. Keep learning: attend field days, listen to radio programs, and join online forums. Some research is participatory, meaning you can test new varieties on your farm. For example, the Cassava Weed Management Project in Nigeria involves farmers in testing. If you want to be a lead farmer, contact your local research institute. Adopting new varieties and methods can increase your yield from 10 to 25 tonnes per hectare. Stay curious and adapt.

lessons.title: Developing a Cassava Farm Business Plan
lessons.body: A business plan helps you get funding and manage your farm. Start with a one-page plan. First, state your goal: e.g., produce 20 tonnes of cassava per hectare on 2 hectares. Then list your costs: land preparation ($150/ha), cuttings ($100/ha), labour ($200/ha), fertiliser ($200/ha), and processing equipment ($500). Total for 2 hectares: about $2,300. Next, estimate income: 20 tonnes/ha at $100/tonne = $2,000/ha, so $4,000 for 2 hectares. But if you process into garri, 1 tonne cassava gives 250 kg garri, selling at $1/kg, so $250 per tonne, meaning $5,000 from 20 tonnes. That's better. Include a timeline: land clearing in March, planting in April, weeding in May and July, harvest in 12 months. Identify your market: local traders, garri buyers, or starch factories. Write a simple cash flow showing when you spend and earn. For funding, approach microfinance banks, government schemes (like CBN Anchor Borrowers in Nigeria), or NGOs. Keep records: a notebook for daily expenses and sales. Use a simple app like FarmBook if you have a smartphone. Also, plan for risks: drought, pests, price drops. Mitigate by planting drought-tolerant varieties, using pest control, and storing garri for off-season sales. Review your plan every 3 months. A good plan is realistic and flexible. It turns farming into a business, not just a livelihood.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Sustainable Cassava Production and Innovation

This practical reference module consolidates the core operational knowledge required to run a profitable, climate-resilient cassava enterprise in Africa. It is designed for agripreneurs, farm managers, extension officers, and processors who need actionable guidance rather than theory. Cassava (Manihot esculenta Crantz) is Africa's most important root crop by volume, with Nigeria alone producing over 60 million tonnes annually. Yet yields across the continent average only 8â12 tonnes per hectare, compared to potential yields of 25â40 tonnes per hectare under improved management. Closing this gap is the single largest commercial opportunity in African cassava value chains.

Climate-Smart Cassava Farming Practices

Cassava is naturally drought-tolerant, but climate change is shifting rainfall patterns, intensifying pest pressure, and expanding the range of diseases such as Cassava Brown Streak Disease (CBSD) and Cassava Mosaic Disease (CMD). Climate-smart practice means selecting varieties matched to local agro-ecology, staggering planting to spread risk, and integrating cassava into diversified cropping systems. In East Africa, the deployment of CMD-resistant varieties developed through the NextGen Cassava project has demonstrated yield gains of 30â40% in affected areas.

Key operational practices include:

  • Variety selection: Choose improved varieties with resistance to CMD, CBSD, and cassava bacterial blight. Match maturity class (early 6â9 months, medium 9â12 months, late 12â18 months) to market demand and land availability.
  • Planting window: Plant at the onset of rains when soil moisture is adequate. Avoid planting into waterlogged soils, which promote root rot.
  • Spacing: Use 1 m Ã 0.8 m or 1 m Ã 1 m for root production; closer spacing for high-biomass varieties intended for processing or livestock feed.
  • Intercropping: Legume intercrops (cowpea, groundnut, soybean) fix nitrogen, suppress weeds, and provide early income while cassava establishes.
  • Mulching and cover crops: Retain crop residues and use cover crops such as Mucuna or Pueraria to conserve moisture and build organic matter.

Soil Health and Environmental Sustainability

Cassava is a heavy feeder, particularly of potassium, and continuous monocropping depletes soils rapidly. Sustainable production requires deliberate nutrient management. A 25 t/ha cassava crop removes approximately 60 kg N, 25 kg PâOâ, and 100 kg KâO per hectare. Without replacement, yields decline within three to four cycles.

Practical soil health measures include:

  • Integrated Soil Fertility Management (ISFM): Combine organic inputs (compost, poultry manure, green manure) with targeted mineral fertiliser. Apply potassium-rich fertiliser (e.g., muriate of potash) at 100â150 kg/ha on depleted soils.
  • Crop rotation: Rotate cassava with cereals or legumes to break pest cycles and restore soil structure.
  • Minimum tillage: Reduce soil disturbance to protect organic matter and soil biota, especially on sloping land.
  • Erosion control: Use contour ridges, vetiver grass strips, or living barriers on slopes above 5%.
  • Agroforestry: Integrate nitrogen-fixing trees (e.g., Gliricidia sepium, Leucaena) for biomass and shade management.

Mechanization and Digital Tools in Cassava

Cassava production is labour-intensive, with land preparation, planting, weeding, and harvesting accounting for 60â70% of production costs. Mechanization and digital tools offer significant cost reduction and precision gains.

Mechanization options: Two-row cassava planters, tractor-mounted boom sprayers, and hydraulic cassava harvesters are increasingly available through service providers in Nigeria, Ghana, Tanzania, and Zambia. For smallholders, shared equipment models (e.g., machinery rings, cooperative ownership) reduce capital barriers. The Cassava Mechanisation and Agro-processing Project (CAMAP) in Nigeria demonstrated that mechanized harvesting reduced labour requirements by up to 80% and post-harvest losses by 30%.

Digital tools: Mobile advisory platforms such as the Cassava Disease Diagnostics app (developed by IITA and partners), SMS-based extension services, and farm management software (e.g., FarmDrive, AgroCenta) support decision-making. Soil testing kits and portable NIRS (near-infrared spectroscopy) devices enable rapid quality assessment at farm gate. Drone-based crop monitoring is emerging in commercial operations for early detection of disease and nutrient stress.

Waste Utilization and Circular Economy

Cassava processing generates substantial waste: peels (10â20% of root weight), wastewater (high in cyanogenic glycosides), and bagasse. Traditionally discarded, these streams represent revenue opportunities. Peels can be fermented into animal feed, composted for soil amendment, or processed into biogas. Wastewater from garri processing can be treated anaerobically to produce biogas and reduce environmental pollution. In Nigeria, the Federal Institute of Industrial Research Oshodi (FIIRO) has developed technologies for converting cassava peels into high-quality livestock feed, reducing feed costs by up to 30% for poultry and ruminant farmers.

Business models for waste valorization include:

  • Centralized composting: Collect peels from multiple processors, compost, and sell to peri-urban vegetable farmers.
  • Feed production: Dry, mill, and pelletize peels for sale to livestock feed mills.
  • Biogas: Install anaerobic digesters at medium-to-large processing plants to offset energy costs.
  • Biochar: Pyrolyze woody stems and bagasse for soil amendment and carbon sequestration.

Research and Development Trends

R&D in African cassava is concentrated in a few major networks: IITA, the CGIAR Research Program on Roots, Tubers and Bananas (RTB), the NextGen Cassava project (Cornell University and partners), and national research institutes such as NRCRI (Nigeria), CSIR-CRI (Ghana), and NARO (Uganda). Current trends include:

  • Genomic selection: Accelerating breeding cycles for disease resistance and yield.
  • Gene editing: Targeting reduced cyanide content and improved starch quality.
  • Post-harvest technology: High-quality cassava flour (HQCF) processing, modified atmosphere packaging, and shelf-stable products.
  • Digital phenotyping: Drone and satellite imagery for yield prediction and disease surveillance.
  • Climate resilience: Breeding for heat and drought tolerance, and for adaptation to shifting agro-ecological zones.

Developing a Cassava Farm Business Plan

A cassava farm business plan must be grounded in realistic yield, price, and cost assumptions. Below are two reference data tables to support financial modelling.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING: Cyanide Toxicity in Cassava Processing

Raw cassava roots contain cyanogenic glycosides (linamarin and lotaustralin). Improper processing can leave dangerous cyanide levels, causing acute poisoning (konzo) and long-term neurological damage. Always peel, soak, ferment, and cook cassava thoroughly. Never consume raw or inadequately processed cassava. Wastewater from processing is also toxic to livestock and aquatic life â contain and treat it before discharge. Train all processing staff on cyanide reduction protocols and provide protective equipment.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Select improved, disease-resistant cassava varieties suited to your agro-ecological zone and market.
  • â Test soil before planting; apply potassium and organic matter based on results.
  • â Plant at onset of rains with certified, disease-free stem cuttings.
  • â Implement at least two weed control cycles and monitor for CMD, CBSD, and pests.
  • â Plan for mechanization or shared equipment to reduce labour costs.
  • â Establish a waste utilization stream (compost, feed, or biogas) from day one.
  • â Maintain records of all costs, yields, and sales for financial analysis.
  • â Train all staff on cyanide safety and proper processing protocols.

Further Reading

  • IITA Cassava Research Portal â technical guides, varieties, and agronomy resources.
  • FAO Cassava Programme â global and regional cassava production and market data.
  • NextGen Cassava Project â breeding innovations and improved variety releases.
  • CGIAR Roots, Tubers and Bananas (RTB) Programme â research briefs and value chain tools.
  • IFAD Cassava Value Chain Development â business model and market access guidance.

This module is part of the Rise AFRICA Skills programme. Always verify local prices, regulations, and variety recommendations with national extension services before making investment decisions.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a drought-tolerant cassava variety?
quiz.explanation: All three varieties are known for drought tolerance and high yields.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for sole cassava planting?
quiz.explanation: 1m x 1m is the standard spacing for sole cassava to allow proper growth.

quiz.q: Which practice helps reduce evaporation and fix nitrogen?
quiz.explanation: Intercropping with legumes like cowpea covers soil and fixes nitrogen.

quiz.q: What is a climate-smart practice for cassava farming?
quiz.explanation: Minimum tillage keeps soil carbon and reduces greenhouse gas emissions.

quiz.explanation: TMS 91/02324 matures in 9-12 months and is suitable for dry areas.

quiz.explanation: Cassava grows best at pH 5.5-6.5; below 5.0 requires liming.

quiz.explanation: Apply 1-2 tonnes per hectare to raise pH to optimal levels.

quiz.explanation: Legumes like soybean fix nitrogen, improving soil fertility.

quiz.explanation: Burning destroys organic matter, kills microbes, and pollutes air.

quiz.q: What is a recommended practice to control erosion in cassava farms?
quiz.explanation: Contour planting slows water runoff and reduces soil erosion.

quiz.explanation: The IITA motorised planter is efficient, planting 1 hectare in 4 hours.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of a tractor-mounted cassava harvester?
quiz.explanation: Mechanical harvesters greatly reduce labour and time.

quiz.q: Which digital tool provides weather forecasts for farmers?

quiz.explanation: Dried cassava peels contain about 10-12% protein.

quiz.q: What can be recovered from cassava processing wastewater?

quiz.q: What is a circular economy approach for cassava waste?
quiz.explanation: Circular economy turns waste into useful products, reducing pollution.
